citations.title: Ml Lecture Notes
citations.text: 5. Data Splitting and Cross-Validation Data is usually divided into a training set for fitting, a validation set for tuning hyperparameters and a test set used once for the final unbiased estimate. Using the test set repeatedly for decisions leaks information and makes the estimate optimistic. Data leakage more generally means that information from outside the training data, such as future values or the target itself, influences the features; it produces unrealistically good scores that collapse in production. k-fold cross-validation splits the training data into k equal folds. The model is trained k times, each time holding out a different fold for validation, and the k scores are averaged. Typical values are k = 5 or k = 10. Stratified k-fold preserves the class proportions in every fold and is recommended for classification with imbalanced classes.

citations.title: Ml Project Handbook
citations.text:
Evaluation Protocol v2
Evaluation protocol v2 supersedes protocol v1 for all projects started in 2025. Split the data 70% training, 15% validation and 15% test. Use k = 5 folds for cross-validation and report the mean and standard deviation of the fold scores. Set random_state=42 everywhere. The test set may be used exactly once. The primary metric is F1 for imbalanced data and accuracy otherwise.

citations.text:
Dropout and choosing between methods
5. Choosing between methods L2 and early stopping are complementary and are often combined.
Early stopping is cheapest; L2 gives a smoother, more reproducible solution. Compare methods by
validation accuracy, never by training accuracy.

citations.title: Ml Reference Notes
citations.text: training and validation data because the model is too simple. Bias: error from wrong or overly simple assumptions.  Variance: error from sensitivity to the specific training sample. Cross-validation: repeated training on different train/validation splits to estimate performance reliably. Data leakage: using information during training that would not be available at prediction time. Confusion matrix: a table of TP, FP, TN and FN counts. Precision: TP / (TP + FP). Recall: TP / (TP + FN). F1: harmonic mean of precision and recall. ROC AUC: area under the receiver operating characteristic curve; 0.5 means random ranking. Imbalanced data: classes occur with very different frequencies. One-hot encoding: representing a category as a binary vector with a single 1. Standardization: rescaling to mean 0 and standard deviation 1.

citations.title: Ml Reference Notes
citations.text: Feature: an input variable used by a model, for example a person's age. Label or target: the value the model should predict. Hyperparameter: a setting chosen before training, such as the learning rate, tree depth or number of neighbors k. Parameter: a value learned during training, such as the weights of linear regression. Epoch: one full pass through the training data. Batch size: the number of examples used for one gradient update. Learning rate: the step size of gradient descent. Regularization: a penalty that discourages overly complex models. L2 (ridge) shrinks weights; L1 (lasso) can set weights to zero. Overfitting: low training error but high validation error because the model memorized noise. Underfitting: high error on both training and validation data because the model is too simple. Bias: error from wrong or overly simple assumptions.
